svg.aria-label: Diagram: how AWS Verified Access evaluates an application request, what it asks a trust provider for on each request, and where its policies live. AWS states that Verified Access provides secure access to applications without requiring the use of a virtual private network, and that it evaluates each application request to ensure users can access each application only when they meet the specified security requirements. The contrast AWS draws is that a traditional security model evaluates access once and grants the user access to all applications, whereas Verified Access evaluates each application access request in real time, which makes it difficult for bad actors to move from one application to another. The mechanism is that when a user tries to access an application, Verified Access gets their data from the trust provider and evaluates it against the policies set for that application, That describes the flow but does not guarantee a fresh fetch from the original source on every request: trust data arrives on a session whose default duration is one day for trust providers created from 24 February 2025, seven days for providers created before that date, or the expiry of a refresh token where one is specified. Per-request authorisation and per-request freshness are therefore different guarantees, and the documentation supports only the first. The trust data itself is obtained from the OIDC provider's UserInfo Endpoint, with the Scope parameter determining which sets are retrieved. Five components make up the service. A Verified Access instance is the resource that organises trust providers and groups, and it evaluates application requests and grants access only when security requirements are met. A Verified Access endpoint represents an application, and the available endpoint types are load balancer, network interface, network CIDR, and Amazon Relational Database Service, where RDS requests go to an RDS instance, cluster or DB proxy, making per-request device-aware access control possible in front of a database rather than only a web application. A Verified Access group is a collection of endpoints, and AWS recommends grouping endpoints for applications with similar security requirements to simplify policy administration. Access policies are user-defined rules determining whether to allow or deny access, specifying a combination of factors including user identity and device security state, and a group access policy is created for each group and inherited by all endpoints in that group, while application-specific policies may optionally be attached to individual endpoints, with each request evaluated against the group policy and any endpoint policies together, which makes an endpoint policy additive rather than a replacement and means the group policy acts as a floor that an endpoint cannot relax. Trust providers are services that manage user identities or device security state, and the data they send is called trust data, also referred to as user claims or trust context, for example a user's email address or a device's operating system version. A critical plumbing asymmetry is that at least one trust provider must be attached to each instance, and an instance accepts a single identity trust provider but multiple device trust providers, so device signals can be plural while the identity source cannot, which means separate directories for contractors or for an acquisition require separate instances with their own groups, endpoints and policies to keep in step. Trust context can include attributes based on user identity such as an email address or membership in a sales organisation, or device information such as installed security patches or anti-virus software version, the latter being the kind of fact a bearer token cannot usefully carry because it changes on a timescale shorter than any sensible token lifetime, and Verified Access supports two categories of trust provider accordingly: user identity providers and device management systems for laptops, tablets and smartphones. On defaults, all application requests are denied by default until a policy is defined, so a newly created endpoint refuses everything until something grants access, and distinguishing a default denial from an evaluated one matters in the same way it does for an authorization decision that returns no determining policy. Verified Access logs all access attempts, not merely successful ones, providing centralised visibility into application access to help respond to security incidents and audit requests, and for a default-deny service the denials carry the signal because that is where a failing device posture or a removed directory membership appears as behaviour rather than as a support ticket. On cost, charging is hourly for each application on Verified Access plus the amount of data processed, two components with different shapes: data processing scales with use, while the per-application hourly charge does not, so an endpoint for an application nobody has opened still bills like one carrying production traffic and decommissioning means deleting the endpoint rather than pointing it nowhere.
svg.title: Authorisation is evaluated per request; the trust data it reads arrives on a session
svg.text: Evaluated every request. Trusted for a day.
AWS Verified Access — per-application evaluation, without a VPN.
The traditional model
“evaluates access once and grants the user
access to all applications”
Network position stands in for authorisation. One
decision at connection time, inherited by everything.
Verified Access
“evaluates each application access request
in real time”
“makes it difficult for bad actors to move from one
application to another” — lateral movement, priced in.
vs
The mechanism, and the half of it that is easy to over-read
“When a user tries to access an application, Verified Access gets their data from the trust provider and
evaluates it against the policies that you set for the application.”
Trust data — and the word AWS uses for it
“Also referred to as user claims or trust context”
identity: email, membership in “sales”
device: “installed security patches or anti-virus
software version”
Same noun as a Cognito claim — and arriving on a session, like one.
The plumbing asymmetry that sets your topology
“a single identity trust provider and multiple
device trust providers” per instance
Device signals plural. Identity singular.
Contractors in another directory = a second instance, with its
own groups, endpoints and policies to keep in step.
Two policies, evaluated together — so the group is a floor
Group policy — written once, “inherited by all endpoints in the group”
Endpoint policy — “optionally” attached to one application, and additive
“evaluates the request against the access policy for the group and any application-specific endpoint policies”
So “this one app needs to be looser” is an argument for a different group, never for an endpoint policy.
The confusing first hour
“All application requests are denied by default,
until a policy is defined.”
Correct default. Your first test fails, and nothing is broken.
Which is why logging comes first
“Verified Access logs all access attempts”
All attempts, not all grants. For a default-deny service the
denials carry the signal — and separate the two kinds of no.
Four endpoint types — and one is a database
load balancer · network interface · network CIDR
RDS instance, cluster, or DB proxy
The bastion-host problem, answered per request.
Two cost shapes, only one scales with use
“charged hourly for each application” + data processed
An endpoint nobody has opened since March bills like one
carrying production traffic. Decommission = delete it.
Every bearer token and VPN session in this series is a variation on “evaluates access once”. This is the first thing built to refuse it.
The price: live dependence on a trust provider per request, one directory per instance, and an hourly line item per application.
